summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning to recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³ (e.g. 49 = 7² = 7×7; 4³ = 64 = 4×4×4). The central aim is to tie the notation to its geometric meaning: n² is the area of an n×n square and n³ is the volume of an n×n×n cube — this is where 'squared' and 'cubed' get their names. The most important misconception to defeat is reading the exponent as a multiplier (7² as 7×2 = 14, or 4³ as 4×3 = 12); anchoring to the square and cube arrays blocks it. Square numbers also lie on the diagonal of the multiplication table (products of equal factors) and have an odd number of factors. Learners should recall the first ~10 squares and the small cubes and use correct notation.
misconceptions: Reading n² as n×2 (7²=14) and n³ as n×3 (4³=12).
Confusing squared and cubed, or the notation ²/³.
Thinking of square/cube numbers as arbitrary lists rather than areas/volumes.
Believing squaring always makes a much bigger number without the geometric picture (surprised by 1²=1).
Not recognising square numbers as products of a number with itself (table diagonal).

activities.title: Growing squares: why 7² is not 7×2
steps: Build or draw an n×n square array for a chosen n and count the total cells, writing it as n².
Start small and step n up: 1 (1 cell), 2 (a 2×2 of 4), 3 (a 3×3 of 9), 4 (a 4×4 of 16). Write each as 1², 2², 3², 4².
Build a 7×7 square (49 cells) and, beside it, a separate 7×2 rectangle (14 cells); compare the two by eye — note that 7² = 49 is far larger than 7×2 = 14.
Say out loud what the little 2 means: 'how many 7s are multiplied together', i.e. 7×7, NOT 'multiply 7 by 2'.
Notice how much is added each time n grows by one: the totals jump 1, 4, 9, 16, and the gaps are 3, 5, 7 — successive odd numbers.
Plot each square number onto the diagonal of a multiplication table (where the row number equals the column number) and see that square numbers are the products of a number with itself.

Optionally notice that a square number has an odd number of factors — e.g. 9 has factors 1, 3, 9 (three of them) — because its square root is a repeated factor that pairs with itself instead of a different partner.
activities.insight: n² means an n×n square array (its area), not n×2. The notation is a picture of a square, and square numbers are the products of equal factors that lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.

activities.title: Building a cube: what 'cubed' really means
steps: Using unit cubes (physical or a build-it model), assemble an n×n×n cube for a chosen n, stacking it layer by layer (each layer is n×n). Keep a running total, and when all n layers are in place write the final total as n×n×n = n³.
Build 4³ specifically: make four layers, each a 4×4 square of 16 cubes, to reach 64 cubes total; write 4³ = 4×4×4 = 64.
Rotate or turn the cube to see all its faces and confirm it is genuinely three-dimensional.
Place a flat 4×4 square (16) beside the 4×4×4 cube (64) and describe the difference: squared uses two equal factors (a flat area), cubed uses three (a solid volume).
Say what the little 3 means: 'how many 4s are multiplied together' — 4×4×4 — not 'multiply 4 by 3'.
activities.insight: n³ means an n×n×n cube built from unit cubes (its volume), using three equal factors. 'Cubed' is spatial and distinct from 'squared'; the exponent counts how many equal factors are multiplied.

activities.title: Reading and recalling the notation
steps: Match notation to meaning and value: 7² ↔ a 7×7 array ↔ 49; 4³ ↔ a 4×4×4 cube ↔ 64. For each, first predict, then reveal the picture and the value.
Answer the question 'why is 7² not 14?' in your own words, referring to the 7×7 square.
List the first ten square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100) and write each with its notation (e.g. 49 = 7²).
Recall the small cubes (1³=1, 2³=8, 3³=27, 4³=64, 5³=125) and write each as repeated equal multiplication.
Write a value using correct notation, e.g. record 49 as 7² (not only as 7×7).
activities.insight: Fluent recall and correct reading of ² and ³ rest on the array/cube meaning; the notation is shorthand for repeated equal multiplication, not a multiplier.

checkQuestion: What does 4² (four squared) equal? And what does 4³ (four cubed) equal? For each, explain what the little raised number is telling you to do — not just the answer.
checkAnswer: 4² = 16 and 4³ = 64. A child reasoning correctly reads 4² as 4 × 4 (four rows of four — a square) and 4³ as 4 × 4 × 4 (a 4-by-4-by-4 cube), explaining the exponent as HOW MANY times the base is used as a factor — not as multiply-by-2 or multiply-by-3.
